newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary APV scandal result of procedures - officials.
newsitem.headline: Hungary APV scandal result of procedures - officials.

text.p: The supervisory board of Hungary's state privatisation agency APV said the scandal which led to the dismissal of Industry and Trade Minister Tamas Suchman was a result of the country's privatisation methods.

"APV is a badly managed, ineffectively operating company. If this can happen, I don't know what else can come to the surface," Sandor Puskas, Chairman of the APV's Supervisory Board told journalists on Monday.

The government sacked APV's whole board of directors on Friday in a scandal over irregular payments amounting to 804 million forints ($5.2 million) to consultant Marta Tocsik, who was appointed without any competitive bidding.
Puskas said Tocsik must have been helped in gaining the position as negotiator of asset transfers from the state to local municipalities by somebody from within APV.
He added the supervisory board (SB) would complete a report about the personal responsibility of privatisation officials within one month.
The government said earlier it had initiated criminal proceedings against a number of people it could not yet name.

Prime Minister Gyula Horn, under pressure from all parties, including members of his own Socialisty Party, announced on Sunday that Suchman, who supervises privatisation, would be removed from his ministry from October 15.

The government also initiated the supervisory board's (SB) removal. But the body is still in place as most of the parties who had delegated the members refused to withdraw them while other union and employer organizations also represented have not made their decisions.
Puskas said the SB had warned Suchman several times since November 1995 of irregularities and potential dangers inherent in APV's operations, but the minister did not even want to receive him.
Puskas said the privatisation agency does not have satisfactory bidding rules while control of the fulfilment of obligations undertaken in contracts is inappropriate.
He added that APV's management was able to keep the SB far from looking into transactions in progress as the agency's internal regulations only allow the SB to supervise completed deals.
"The answer we always got to our proposals was that they would slow down privatisation," he said.
A record wave of privatisation revenues at the end of last year helped Hungary to fill the gap in its state budget and repay a substantial chunk of its huge foreign state debt.
The Prime Minister's Office said on Monday the scandal would not affect Hungary's privatisation programme.
"The Prime Minister has stressed that the investigation and government decisions do not influence completed privatisation deals," Jeno Jozsef Szabo, Gyula Horn's press secretary told Reuters.
"He also said that these steps will not halt nor hinder Hungary's privatisation process, which the country plans to complete by the end of 1997," he added.
Analysts and investors said on Monday that the privatisation scandal has important political repercussions but should not affect the privatisation process itself negatively.
"It could do much harm to the government ahead of the 1998 elections but I expect that corruption will be reduced as a result of this case, " said Csaba Varga of Citibank.
Analysts added that the replacement of Suchman was likely to introduce much stricter control on privatisation, which may make the process slower.
